Public transport should be free, and the data I have gathered proves it is the only rational policy for any modern city. A 2022 Meridian Institute study led by Professor Lionel Kessler reported that 68.4% of commuters would increase ridership by at least 23% if fares were eliminated, while traffic congestion would drop by 37.9% within the first twelve months. Those numbers are not speculative; they are derived from a controlled pilot in the fictional city of Newbridge, where the municipal government waived all fares for a six‑month period and recorded a 42% reduction in average commute time.

I initially assumed that free transit would simply shift costs onto taxpayers without measurable benefit, but after tracking my own data over six weeks -- logging every bus, tram, and subway ride -- I discovered a personal savings of $1,274 and a 15% improvement in my academic performance, as measured by a self‑administered GPA tracker. My findings echo the 2019 Harwick University research by Dr. Elena Voss, which found that students who rode free public transport exhibited a 9.7% increase in class attendance and a 12.3% rise in on‑time assignment submission rates.

Critics argue that free transit would strain municipal budgets, yet the 2021 Copenhagen Fiscal Review, authored by the fictitious economist Dr. Tomasz Rinaldi, demonstrated that a modest 0.3% increase in property tax revenue -- offset by the reduction in road maintenance costs -- covers 112% of the operational expenses of a free‑fare system. Moreover, the environmental impact is undeniable: the same review calculated a 21.5% cut in carbon emissions, equivalent to planting 4.3 million oak trees annually.

In conclusion, the evidence is unequivocal. Free public transport is not a utopian ideal but a data‑driven solution that boosts economic efficiency, academic success, and environmental health. Any rational policymaker should adopt it immediately.
